title: Measuring Coherence in Predictive Models
claim: Approximate models can be incoherent, so objectives that are equivalent under exact inference diverge and select different choices.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, zoomed inset magnifying a density peak in panel (a)
description: Two line-plot panels. Panel (a) plots predictive density against output y*. It shows a dashed blue current predictive P_Y and two solid blue expected future predictives, Q^A_Y (light blue) and Q^B_Y (dark navy). The curves nearly overlap as bell shapes. A gray box on the peak links to a large inset that magnifies it. In the inset, P_Y sits between Q^B_Y above and Q^A_Y below, with the gap shaded light blue, so neither future predictive matches the current one. Panel (b) plots objective in nats against candidate design a. A black curve (exact Bayes, all forms) is a single line. Mean-field EPIG_H (blue), EMI (orange) and EPIG_KL (green dashed) separate from it and from each other. Candidates A and B are marked with dots on each curve. The eye goes first to the inset, then to the diverging curves in (b).
caption: Objective splitting under mean-field VI for Bayesian linear regression. (a) The mean-field model's current predictive \(P_Y\) (dashed) and its expected future predictives \(Q^A_Y\) and \(Q^B_Y\) after acquiring candidates \(A\) and \(B\). The inset magnifies the peak, where neither expected future predictive matches the current one, so the model is incoherent for both candidates. (b) The three forms of EPIG against the candidate design \(a\). Under exact Bayes they coincide. Under mean-field VI, \(\EPIG_H\) prefers \(B\) whereas EMI prefers \(A\), and \(\EPIG_{\KL}\) (dashed) stays within 0.002 nats of EMI.
abstract: Many sequential decision-making procedures, such as active learning, implicitly assume that a model's current predictions agree with those it expects to make after updating on new data, a property we call coherence. Most models in use do not update by exact conditioning and are not guaranteed to be coherent, which can lead to worse decisions. Yet there is currently no general way to measure incoherence or to tell when it matters. We develop tools to measure incoherence and characterise when it affects decisions. We introduce the incoherence ratio, an MMD-based measure of how far any updating procedure departs from coherence, computed only from the procedure's own predictions and updates, and accompany it with an anytime-valid test of coherence. In Bayesian experimental design, acquisition objectives that are equivalent for coherent models choose different data under every approximate model we study, and the incoherence ratio tracks how far incoherence distorts them. We also introduce action coherence, which captures only the incoherence that changes a decision. What a resulting disagreement costs, however, is determined primarily by predictive accuracy. Sequential decisions depend on how a model updates as well as on what it predicts, so coherence, like accuracy, should be checked rather than assumed.
